anomaly_def.Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine and its sessions consume more physical or virtual memory than the host can safely supply, provoking paging, OOM events, and cache-churn. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby, replica, or downstream consumers fall behind the primary because they cannot receive or apply log records at the production rate, widening log-position gaps and retaining log files. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space for data, log, temp, or backup areas falls to—or reaches—hard limits, producing allocation failures and preventing further growth or recycling.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: sustained OS memory pressure and swap storms slow both primary and replica processes; replication lag grows rapidly, causing ever-larger piles of unrecycled WAL/redo or relay logs; the ballooning log archives, combined with already constrained data, temp, and backup areas, drive the platform toward disk-full conditions. As space dwindles, checkpoints, autovacuum/clean-up jobs, temporary-object creation, and even normal DML may stall or error. Simultaneously, memory exhaustion can trigger process restarts that reset replication connections, further enlarging the backlog, while replicas under memory stress replay logs even more slowly, compounding lag metrics. Operations teams may see erratic query latency, intermittent OOM terminations, mounting replication delays, and cascading "out of space" or "cannot allocate" errors across primary and secondary nodes.

Causal chain: excessive memory allocation on the primary (and potentially replicas) reduces CPU throughput and elevates checkpoint frequency as dirty buffers are flushed under pressure. The slower checkpoint and apply throughput make replicas lag, which forces the primary to retain additional WAL segments. These retained logs, together with memory-induced delays in maintenance tasks (vacuum, purge, backup copy/move), accelerate consumption of storage capacity. As disk space nears exhaustion, background writers and archivers stall, which in turn increases in-memory pressure because buffers cannot be flushed or freed promptly. The interlocking feedback—memory overcommitment slowing replication, replication backlog inflating disk usage, and disk saturation inhibiting memory relief—drives the database into a critical state that threatens availability and data protection.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
